extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy writers (open-mic/new comics) seeking to write stronger jokes
extracted.subtask_description: A practical blueprint for writing jokes for stand-up: pick a non-funny premise, set a clean setup that points to a norm, then deliver a clever, benign twist and tag it. Focused on building tension and preserving surprise so punchlines land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise must not be a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: The premise is not a joke — it’s a frustration, fear, confession, or flaw tied to a topic. You’re not trying to be clever yet; you’re stating the emotional truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the premise vulnerable and disarming so the audience leans in and expects sincerity. Example: 'I’m not looking for pity, but just so you’re aware—' is non-funny and curious. Anti-pattern: putting a joke in the premise (e.g., 'I’ve got the body of a Greek god and the butt of a Ken doll') which gives the punchline away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your Comedy Lens (on‑brand POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Comedy Lens is how you view the world — your internal logic, quirks, and consistent persona that makes lines feel authentic to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a take that is on-brand so the audience believes the twist came from you. Example: the author’s 'Clumsy Aspy-hole' persona makes 'I was born without an ass' land as believable and character-driven. This increases payoff because the laugh is tied to a trusted POV rather than a random gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup: point to a norm and include zero jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The setup should set an expectation by cleanly indicating a norm — a common belief, pattern, or social rule — and must contain no jokes or chuckle crumbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clean on-ramp that baitsthe audience toward a sincere expectation (e.g., 'I am handicapped.'). Do not add one-liners, fluff, or self-sabotaging asides in the setup (anti-pattern: 'I’m handicapped—emotionally, financially, and spiritually, haha!'). The setup should not telegraph the punchline; it should build quiet tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection should bait, not mock or trick
rubrics_metrics.description: Misdirection is achieved by guiding the audience to assume a particular, often serious, direction so the twist flips that expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bait the audience using shared assumptions 'just far enough' so the eventual flip surprises. Do this ethically — you are baiting expectations, not mocking vulnerable groups. Keep the pre‑flip material clean to preserve the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline: a clever, benign violation of the norm
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline should be a specific, absurd, and benignly violating twist that flips the setup’s expectation and doesn’t harm or alienate the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a punchline that is emotionally connected yet ridiculous (example: 'I was born without an ass.'). Avoid mean or cringey twists. Combine devices like bait & switch, sarcasm, exaggeration, or sexual innuendo deliberately to craft the twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not leak the surprise (no jokes in setup / no early zingers)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you put jokes or 'chuckle crumbs' in the premise or setup, you burn the surprise and reduce the punchline’s impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the setup like loading a slingshot: any premature laughter leaks air. Example anti-pattern: a clever-sounding setup that actually gives away the punchline and turns the joke into a shrug. Final rule reiterated: 'No jokes in the setup. I mean it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag intentionally using Humor Heightening Devices
rubrics_metrics.description: After the punchline, add tags intentionally to heighten the POV and extend the laugh; use one or more of the taught devices rather than random one-liners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tag choices should deepen the audience’s trust in the POV and build the bit instead of chasing immediate laughs. Examples of devices and tags: Exaggeration ('I slide off chairs like a cartoon banana peel.'), Anthropomorphizing ('My jeans are just flapping in back like a bored puppet.'), Fantasy Outlet for Frustration ('If I had a real ass, I’d slam it shut like a filing cabinet.'), Cut Forward To ('Cut to me at TSA getting flagged for “suspicious lack of cheeks.”'). Use tagging to keep the audience hooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 36 Humor Heightening Devices as a toolkit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a (taught) list of 36 humor-heightening devices to mix and match when crafting punchlines and tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select devices that fit your Comedy Lens and the bit’s emotional truth (e.g., bait & switch, sarcasm, exaggeration, sexual innuendo). Combine devices intentionally to heighten rather than to clutter. The devices are tools for engineering jokes and building a sustained bit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build tension through the three-part flow: premise → setup → punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes should be engineered: the premise reveals vulnerability, the setup builds quiet tension and expectation, and the punchline detonates that tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this sequence to 'load the slingshot' and 'earn the explosion' at the end. After the explosion, use tags to exploit the established POV. If a joke isn’t working, check whether the setup leaked the surprise or the premise tried to be funny too early.
